questions.stem: In particle physics, what does applying time-reversal symmetry to a reaction do?
options: Moves one particle to the other side as its antiparticle
Slows the reaction down so that it takes much longer to happen
Runs the reaction backwards, so the products become the reactants
Replaces every particle in the reaction with its antiparticle
questions.explanation: Time-reversal symmetry predicts that if a reaction can happen, the reverse reaction, with the arrow pointing the other way, can also happen. Replacing every particle with its antiparticle is charge-reversal symmetry, and moving one particle across is crossing symmetry.

questions.stem: What does applying charge-reversal symmetry to a reaction do?
options: Swaps the reactants and the products of the reaction around
Replaces every charged particle with a neutral one
Replaces every particle in the reaction with its antiparticle
Changes the sign of the charge on the reactants only, not the products
questions.explanation: Charge-reversal symmetry swaps every particle, on both sides, for its antiparticle. That reverses every charge, baryon number and lepton number, so a reaction that conserved them still does. Swapping reactants and products is time reversal.

questions.stem: What does crossing symmetry allow you to do to a particle reaction?
options: Swap any quark for a lepton with the same charge
Move one particle to the other side, changing it to its antiparticle
Move one particle to the other side, keeping it the same particle
Swap every particle for its antiparticle on both sides of the arrow
questions.explanation: Crossing symmetry moves a single particle across the arrow, and it must become its antiparticle when it crosses. Moving it unchanged would break charge and lepton or baryon number conservation. Swapping every particle is charge reversal.

questions.stem: In beta-minus decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. What reaction does time-reversal symmetry predict?
options: p → n + e⁺ + νₑ
p + e⁺ + νₑ → n
p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ → n
n̄ → p̄ + e⁺ + νₑ
questions.explanation: Time reversal runs the reaction backwards: the products p, e⁻ and ν̄ₑ become the reactants and n becomes the product. This is a reaction that turns a proton into a neutron. Swapping particles for antiparticles is charge reversal, which gives the antineutron decay.

questions.stem: In beta-minus decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. What reaction does charge-reversal symmetry predict?
options: n̄ → p̄ + e⁺ + νₑ
p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ → n
n → p̄ + e⁺ + ν̄ₑ
n̄ → p + e⁻ + νₑ
questions.explanation: Charge reversal replaces every particle with its antiparticle: the neutron becomes an antineutron, the proton an antiproton, the electron a positron and the electron antineutrino an electron neutrino. The result is the decay of an antineutron. Changing only some of the particles breaks the conservation laws.

questions.stem: Crossing symmetry is applied to the antineutrino in beta-minus decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ, moving it to the left-hand side. What reaction results?
options: ν̄ₑ + n → p + e⁻
νₑ + p → n + e⁻
n → p + e⁻ + νₑ
νₑ + n → p + e⁻
questions.explanation: Crossing moves the antineutrino to the reactants as its antiparticle, the electron neutrino: νₑ + n → p + e⁻. Lepton number balances: 1 on the left and 1 for the electron on the right. Moving it unchanged would give lepton number −1 on the left and +1 on the right.

questions.stem: Symmetry applied to beta-minus decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ, predicts reactions that turn a proton into a neutron. Which of these is one?
options: p + e⁻ → n + ν̄ₑ
p → n + e⁻ + νₑ
p + e⁺ → n + ν̄ₑ
p + e⁻ → n + νₑ
questions.explanation: Time reversal gives p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ → n; crossing the antineutrino to the right as a neutrino gives p + e⁻ → n + νₑ, which is electron capture. Charge (+1 − 1 = 0), baryon number (1 = 1) and lepton number (1 = 1) all balance. The antineutrino version has lepton number 1 on the left and −1 on the right.

questions.stem: Applying symmetry to beta-minus decay also predicts beta-plus decay, p → n + e⁺ + νₑ. Which quantities does this reaction conserve?
options: Charge and baryon number, but not lepton number
Baryon number and lepton number, but not charge
Charge and lepton number, but not baryon number
Charge, baryon number and lepton number
questions.explanation: Charge: +1 = 0 + 1 + 0. Baryon number: 1 = 1. Lepton number: 0 = −1 + 1, since the positron is an antilepton and the neutrino is a lepton. A reaction made by applying the symmetry rules correctly always conserves all three.

questions.stem: Symmetry predicts p → n + e⁺ + νₑ, yet free protons are never seen to decay this way. It happens only for protons inside certain nuclei. Why?
options: Free protons have no quarks that the weak force can change
A neutron has more mass than a proton, so a free proton lacks the energy
Beta-plus decay breaks lepton number conservation outside a nucleus
The strong force stops free protons from emitting positrons at all
questions.explanation: Symmetry shows which reactions conserve charge, baryon and lepton number, but energy must also be conserved. The neutron's mass is greater than the proton's, so a free proton cannot decay into one. Inside a proton-rich nucleus the change in binding energy can supply the difference.

questions.stem: Electron-positron annihilation is e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ. What reaction does time-reversal symmetry predict?
options: γ → e⁻ + e⁻
e⁻ + γ → e⁺ + γ
γ + γ → e⁻ + e⁺
e⁺ + e⁻ → γ + γ
questions.explanation: Reversing the reaction gives two photons producing an electron-positron pair, which is pair production. Charge and lepton number are zero on both sides. Writing the reactants in a different order is the same reaction, not a new one.

questions.stem: A muon decays by μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + νμ. Which decay does charge-reversal symmetry predict?
options: μ⁺ → e⁺ + νₑ + ν̄μ
μ⁺ → e⁺ + ν̄ₑ + νμ
μ⁻ → e⁺ + νₑ + ν̄μ
e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + νμ → μ⁻
questions.explanation: Charge reversal swaps every particle for its antiparticle: the muon becomes an antimuon, the electron a positron, and each neutrino or antineutrino becomes its opposite. The reversed reaction with the arrow turned around is time reversal. This antimuon decay is observed.

questions.stem: Applying crossing symmetry to beta-minus decay, a student writes n → p + e⁻ + νₑ. Why is this reaction impossible?
options: Baryon number is 1 before and 2 after, so it is not conserved
Neutrinos can never be produced in the decay of a neutron
Lepton number is 0 before and 2 after, so it is not conserved
Charge is 0 before and +2 after, so it is not conserved
questions.explanation: The electron and the electron neutrino each have lepton number +1, so the products total 2 while the neutron has 0. Charge balances (0 = +1 − 1 + 0) and so does baryon number. The real decay has an antineutrino, with lepton number −1.

questions.stem: Why must a particle become its antiparticle when crossing symmetry moves it to the other side of a reaction?
options: So that charge, baryon number and lepton number stay conserved
So that the total mass on each side of the reaction is equal
So that the number of particles on each side stays the same
So that the reaction can only proceed through the strong force
questions.explanation: A particle's charge, baryon number and lepton number count positive on one side of the arrow. Moving it across as its antiparticle, with opposite values, keeps every total balanced. Rest mass need not balance, and the particle count changes when one particle moves across.

questions.stem: What do high-energy particle accelerators do to test theories such as the Standard Model?
options: Separate atoms into their elements by their different masses and charges
Store antimatter so that its properties can be studied at rest
Give charged particles huge energies and collide them to study the products
Slow charged particles down until they can be weighed directly on scales
questions.explanation: Accelerators raise charged particles to very high kinetic energies and collide them. The collision energy can create new particles, whose decays are recorded by detectors and compared with the theory's predictions.

questions.stem: In a modern particle accelerator, what increases the particles' kinetic energy?
options: Detectors placed around the collision point
Electric fields in radio-frequency cavities
Strong magnetic fields in bending magnets
Gravitational fields along the beam pipe
questions.explanation: An electric field pushes a charged particle along its direction of motion, doing work on it. The magnets steer and focus the beam but cannot speed it up. Gravity is far too weak to matter.

questions.stem: Why can the magnets in a circular accelerator steer the particles but not increase their speed?
options: The magnetic force acts along the velocity but is far too weak to matter
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
The magnetic force acts only on particles that are moving slowly, not fast ones
The magnetic force is cancelled by the particles' own magnetic fields
questions.explanation: The force on a moving charge, F = qvB, acts at right angles to its velocity. A force perpendicular to the motion changes its direction but does no work, so the speed and kinetic energy stay the same. That is the condition for circular motion.

questions.stem: In a synchrotron, particles travel around a ring of fixed radius. Why must the magnetic field be increased as the particles gain energy?
options: Their mass falls, so a stronger field is needed to stop them escaping
Their momentum rises, so a stronger field is needed to keep r = mv/(qB) fixed
Their charge rises, so a stronger field is needed to hold them in the ring
Their speed falls, so a stronger field is needed to keep them moving
questions.explanation: Setting qvB = mv²/r gives r = mv/(qB), so the radius is proportional to momentum for a given field. As the particles gain momentum, B must rise in step to keep the radius fixed. Their charge never changes, and their momentum rises.

questions.stem: Why can only charged particles be accelerated directly in a particle accelerator?
options: Neutral particles already travel at the speed of light
Charged particles are the only ones with kinetic energy
Electric and magnetic forces act only on charged particles
Neutral particles have far too much mass for any field to accelerate
questions.explanation: Accelerators use electric fields to speed particles up and magnetic fields to steer them, and both forces act only on charge. Neutral particles, such as neutrons, can only be made as products of collisions involving charged particles.

questions.stem: Why have higher-energy accelerators been able to discover heavier particles?
options: Higher energies split the heavy particles out of the protons they hide in
By E = mc², more collision energy can be turned into more rest mass
Higher energies make the existing particles permanently heavier
Heavier particles are only stable at high temperatures
questions.explanation: Mass-energy equivalence means kinetic energy in a collision can become the rest mass of new particles. A particle of mass m needs at least mc² of available energy. That is why the Higgs boson, with a mass about 130 times the proton's, needed the energies of the Large Hadron Collider.

questions.stem: A gamma-ray photon produces an electron-positron pair. What is the least energy the photon must have? Electron mass = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The photon must supply the rest energy of two particles, each of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg: E = 2mc² = 2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. Using one particle gives 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, and multiplying by c rather than c² gives 5.5 × 10⁻²² J.

questions.stem: Why must accelerators reach higher energies to probe smaller structures, such as the inside of a proton?
options: Higher momentum gives a shorter de Broglie wavelength, resolving finer detail
Higher energy makes the target particles swell, so they are larger and easier to see
Higher energy slows the particles so they spend longer near the target
Higher momentum gives a longer de Broglie wavelength, reaching further in
questions.explanation: A probe can resolve detail only about as small as its wavelength, and λ = h/p falls as momentum rises. To see inside a proton, about 10⁻¹⁵ m across, the probe's wavelength must be smaller than that, which needs very high momentum.

questions.stem: A proton in an accelerator has momentum 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength, and could it resolve structure inside a proton about 10⁻¹⁵ m across? h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
options: 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ m, so yes, it is smaller than the proton
6.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ m, so no, it is larger than the proton
1.5 × 10¹⁵ m, so no, it is far larger than the proton
6.6 × 10⁻⁵² m, so yes, it is far smaller than the proton
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/1.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ m, which is smaller than 10⁻¹⁵ m, so it can resolve structure inside the proton. Inverting the fraction gives 1.5 × 10¹⁵ m, and multiplying gives 6.6 × 10⁻⁵² m.

questions.stem: Why do modern colliders smash two beams together head-on rather than firing one beam at a stationary target?
options: Head-on collisions double the particles' charge, so they interact more
A stationary target absorbs the beam before any collisions occur
Head-on collisions remove the need for any magnets to steer the beams
With zero total momentum, more of the energy can become new particles
questions.explanation: When a beam hits a fixed target, momentum must be conserved, so much of the energy stays as kinetic energy of the products. Two equal beams colliding head-on have zero total momentum, so nearly all their energy is available to make new particles.

questions.stem: Which discovery at the Large Hadron Collider, announced in 2012, confirmed a key prediction of the Standard Model?
options: The Higgs boson
The electron
The neutron
The muon neutrino
questions.explanation: The ATLAS and CMS experiments announced the discovery of the Higgs boson on 4 July 2012. The Standard Model had predicted it decades earlier as part of how particles gain mass. The electron, neutron and muon neutrino were all known decades before the Large Hadron Collider was built.

questions.stem: The theory uniting the electromagnetic and weak forces predicted heavy force carriers. How was this tested?
options: Gluons were detected leaving protons in low-energy scattering experiments
Photons were shown to carry the weak force in beta decay experiments
Neutrinos were found to carry the electromagnetic force in reactors
The W and Z bosons were produced in collider experiments at CERN in 1983
questions.explanation: Electroweak theory predicted the W⁺, W⁻ and Z bosons with masses roughly 85 to 100 times the proton's. Proton-antiproton collisions at CERN produced them in 1983. Gluons carry the strong force and photons the electromagnetic force.

questions.stem: In the late 1960s, electrons from the Stanford linear accelerator were scattered off protons, and some were scattered through much larger angles than expected. What did this show?
options: Protons are held together by electrons orbiting inside the nucleus
Protons contain small, point-like charged parts, later identified as quarks
Protons are solid, uniform spheres of charge with no internal structure
Electrons are made of quarks that interact with the proton's quarks
questions.explanation: Large-angle scattering meant the electrons were hitting small, hard concentrations of charge inside the proton, much as Rutherford's alpha particles revealed the nucleus. These were identified as quarks. Electrons are leptons with no known parts.

questions.stem: In a particle detector inside a magnetic field, two particles with the same charge leave curved tracks. One curves much more tightly. What does this show?
options: The tightly curving particle has more momentum
The tightly curving particle has the opposite charge
The tightly curving particle has no charge at all
The tightly curving particle has less momentum
questions.explanation: From r = mv/(qB), the radius is proportional to momentum for the same charge and field, so a tighter curve means less momentum. Opposite charges would curve in opposite directions, and a neutral particle leaves no curved track.

questions.stem: Why are the largest accelerators, such as the Large Hadron Collider, built and run by many countries together?
options: Only one country in the world has the expertise to design the magnets
Particle beams must cross national borders to reach full speed
Their cost and scientific scale are too great for most single nations
International law forbids any nation from running an accelerator
questions.explanation: Large-scale facilities cost billions of dollars and need thousands of scientists and engineers. Sharing the cost and the data through international collaboration makes such projects possible and allows results to be checked by independent teams.

questions.stem: According to the Standard Model and Big Bang theory, how did the four fundamental forces behave in the earliest moments of the universe?
options: They are thought to have acted as one unified force, then separated as it cooled
They had their present strengths from the start and have not changed since
Only gravity existed, and the other forces were created by the first stars
Each force was carried by the same gauge boson until the first atoms formed
questions.explanation: At the extreme temperatures just after the Big Bang the forces are thought to have been unified. As the universe expanded and cooled, they separated one by one into the four forces seen today. Stars came much later.

questions.stem: In which order are the fundamental forces thought to have separated from the unified force after the Big Bang?
options: The weak force, then the strong force, then gravity and the electromagnetic force
Gravity, then the strong force, then the weak and electromagnetic forces
The electromagnetic force, then the weak force, then gravity and the strong force
The strong force, then gravity, then the weak and electromagnetic forces
questions.explanation: Gravity separated first, then the strong force, and the electromagnetic and weak forces stayed unified as the electroweak force until last. That final separation happened at energies that colliders can reach, which is why the W and Z bosons could be produced and studied.

questions.stem: In the first millionth of a second or so, quarks moved freely in a hot 'quark-gluon plasma'. Why did protons and neutrons form only later?
options: Once it had cooled enough, the strong force could bind quarks into hadrons
Once it had cooled enough, the weak force could turn leptons into quarks
Once electrons existed, they could hold the quarks together in groups
Once gravity separated, it could pull quarks together into nucleons
questions.explanation: At very high temperatures the quarks had too much energy to stay bound. As the universe cooled, the strong force, carried by gluons, confined them into hadrons such as protons and neutrons. Gravity is far too weak to bind quarks.

questions.stem: How does the Standard Model describe the creation of matter in the early universe?
options: High-energy photons formed particle-antiparticle pairs, most of which then annihilated
Matter was made in the cores of the very first stars from their gravitational energy
Equal amounts of matter and antimatter formed and then never met one another again
Gluons combined in pairs to form the protons and electrons seen today
questions.explanation: When the universe was hot enough, photon energy turned into particle-antiparticle pairs, and pairs annihilated back into photons. As it cooled, pair production stopped and most matter and antimatter annihilated, leaving a small excess of matter that makes up everything today.

questions.stem: Which of these questions about the early universe does the Standard Model not yet fully answer?
options: Why particle-antiparticle pairs annihilate into photons
Why slightly more matter than antimatter remained
Why quarks combined into protons and neutrons
Why the W and Z bosons have mass but the photon does not
questions.explanation: The Standard Model allows a small difference between matter and antimatter, but not enough to explain the excess that survived. It does explain quark confinement by the strong force, the W and Z masses through the Higgs field, and annihilation into photons.

questions.stem: Which elements were made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang?
options: Mainly carbon, oxygen and iron
All of the elements up to uranium, in equal amounts
Only hydrogen, with no heavier elements
Mainly hydrogen and helium, with a trace of lithium
questions.explanation: In the first few minutes, protons and neutrons fused to make helium nuclei, with small amounts of deuterium and lithium; most protons were left as hydrogen nuclei. The universe then became too cool and spread out for further fusion. Heavier elements were made later in stars.

questions.stem: When nuclei began to form after the Big Bang, there was about one neutron for every seven protons. If all the neutrons ended up in helium-4 nuclei (2 protons and 2 neutrons), about what fraction of the mass was helium?
questions.explanation: Take 2 neutrons and 14 protons, 16 nucleons. The 2 neutrons pair with 2 protons to make one helium-4 nucleus of 4 nucleons, so helium is 4/16 = 25% of the mass. This prediction matches the helium measured in gas clouds with very few heavier elements, supporting the theory.

questions.stem: Some accelerators collide heavy nuclei, such as lead, at very high energies. How does this help test the Standard Model's account of the early universe?
options: It briefly recreates the quark-gluon plasma of the first microseconds
It creates new stars that show how the first elements were made
It separates gravity from the other forces so it can be measured
It slows down the expansion of the universe inside the detector
questions.explanation: The collisions produce a tiny region hot and dense enough for quarks and gluons to move freely, as they did in the first microseconds. Studying how it forms and cools tests the theory. No collider can reach the energies at which gravity is thought to separate.

questions.stem: Which observation is evidence for the Big Bang theory?
options: The steady brightness of the Sun over time
The tides caused by the Moon
The solar wind reaching Earth each day
The cosmic microwave background radiation
questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background is radiation left from when the universe first became transparent, stretched to microwave wavelengths by expansion. With the redshift of distant galaxies and the abundance of light elements, it supports the Big Bang. The other observations concern the Solar System.

questions.stem: Free neutrons decay into protons with a half-life of about 10 minutes, while protons are stable. How did this affect the early universe?
options: All neutrons decayed before any nuclei could form, leaving no helium
The neutron-to-proton ratio kept falling until neutrons were bound in nuclei
The neutron-to-proton ratio kept rising until all protons had decayed
The neutron-to-proton ratio stayed fixed, as neutrons were stable then
questions.explanation: Until neutrons were locked into nuclei within the first few minutes, some decayed into protons, lowering the neutron-to-proton ratio. Nuclei formed before most decayed, so neutrons survived in helium. The amount of helium depends on that timing, which is one way the theory is tested.
